rationale: A wins because it gives the founder genuinely different reporting paths instead of reheating the same viability question. Its strongest angle, "Substack wants writers to post video. Whether that helps them or Substack more is the real question," points to a real reported story with creators, economics, and adoption proof. B has usable bones, but "Substack completes its swap from email newsletter to all-in-video media app" overstates the facts before the reporter has even opened the notebook.
gaps_in_A: "The prevailing belief, widely published since 2022-2023" is outside the supplied update. The subscription-fatigue frame may be true, but this set needs a citation or softer language.

"implying $40M or more flowed to Substack from top creators alone" is a tempting back-of-napkin line, but it depends on whether the $400M is gross subscription revenue or creator net earnings. Flagged later, but too confidently stated in the angle.
"a specific writer with 10,000 paid subscribers" is an invented illustrative customer. Make it explicitly hypothetical or cut the number.
gaps_in_B: "Substack completes its swap from email newsletter to all-in-video media app" is sloppy overclaiming. Native video does not mean the company is now "all-in-video" or has "completed" anything.
"short-form, algorithmic-style feed" is not in the facts. "TikTok-style" does not prove short-form video, algorithmic ranking, or open discovery.
"The numbers behind Substack's 'struggling platform' reputation don't add up" overreaches. Creator earnings and paid subscription count do not answer profitability, runway, or valuation pressure.

It refuses "A customer-story angle" only because individual creator earnings are undisclosed, then misses the valid customer story: whether working writers will adopt native video at all. That's the most useful founder-facing angle in this update.
